It has been revealed that shiba Inu (SHIB) gained 5.96% over the past 24 hours and traded at $0.0000038 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap, as talk of a December "Santa rally" returned to the crypto market. Still, SHIB is down 8.86% over the past seven days, and the token has lost 18.5% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

Last week, SHIB dropped to $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021.

According to recent reports, the hopes for a Santa rally come after Goldman Sachs analysts mentioned last week that most of the December gains on the stock market usually come after Dec. 15. SHIB's own December history, however, reveals that the Santa rally came for the token once in five years.

According to CryptoRank, SHIB lost 29.5% and 13.5% in December of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In December of 2023, the token gained 24.6%. In December of 2024 and 2025, SHIB lost 21% and 17.6%, respectively.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data.

Recent findings suggest that the green December of 2023 came after SHIB gained 6.04% in October and 6.62% in November of that year, according to CryptoRank. In 2026, SHIB lost 18.6% in October, and November is also in the red so far.

Industry observers note that the Goldman note, titled "GS Flow of Funds: Chopsgiving," came from Gail Hafif, Brian Garrett and Lee Coppersmith, who looked at S&P 500 data going back to 1928. According to the note, the index usually gains 1.1% from mid-November to early December and then gives back about two-thirds of that gain by mid-December, and around 80% of the full 2.4% gain comes after Dec. 14-15.

In a recent development, since 1990, the S&P 500 has risen after Dec. 15 in 27 of 36 years, according to Goldman.

The Goldman team called these figures a historical map. In the years when the VIX volatility index was above 18 in the middle of November, the S&P 500 gained 1.34% on average, and the index ended the year higher in 59% of cases, according to the note. According to Goldman, the VIX was above that level in mid-November of this year as well.

In a recent development, goldman also remarked that retail investors have been buying big tech and chip stocks. Large funds and systematic traders have been cutting their positions, according to the note.

Recent findings suggest that the Stock Trader's Almanac counts the last five trading days of December and the first two trading days of January as the Santa Claus rally. This season, the window will open on Dec. 24 and close on Jan. 5.

In the window that ended on Jan. 5, 2026, the S&P 500 declined 0.11%, according to the Almanac. "Santa was a no-show for the third year in a row," the Almanac wrote. Before that, the S&P 500 also ended the Santa Claus rally windows of 2023 and 2024 lower.

Latest Update: Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.
  • Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.
  • The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm.

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their latest startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

It has been revealed that the new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the manufacturer, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of substantial names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the tech giant-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

Sources indicate that “The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis noted in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”.

It has been revealed that marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis mentioned the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Recent findings suggest that lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight organization acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders noted the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis noted.

In a recent development, since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making upcoming data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The firm isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Sources indicate that its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s latest Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

According to recent reports, both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company states it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Sources indicate that srinivasan remarked that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a fresh AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he stated.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe notes gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders noted. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe intends to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis mentioned. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

Recent findings suggest that the $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking firm DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

According to recent reports, marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis noted the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one significant customer that could pull out.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of upcoming chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

It has been revealed that that detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

Industry observers note that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a latest whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

It has been revealed that two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

Industry observers note that that sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain claims it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain indicates the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange consumers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

It has been revealed that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain states it will announce any change to the process in advance.

According to recent reports, the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

It has been revealed that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Industry observers note that taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son vowed tonight to “double down” on its investment in WeWork as he confirmed intends for a $9.5 billion rescue package that will provide up to $1.7 billion to WeWork cofounder Adam Neumann in exchange for cutting most ties with the company and will give SoftBank an 80 percent stake in the business. In a statement tonight in Upcoming York, SoftBank said it would “accelerate” WeWork’s path to profitability and positive free cash flow. More here in the Financial Times.

In a recent development, forty-six attorneys general have joined a Upcoming York-led antitrust investigation of Facebook, officials declared this morning, raising the stakes in a sweeping bipartisan probe that could result in massive changes to the company’s business practices. The Washington Post has more here.

Industry observers note that limited partners or LPs  — the pension funds, the university endowments, the family offices that largely provide venture firms with their spending money — are receiving a lot of attention from venture capitalists, some of it unwanted. VCs have begun knocking down their doors with requests for fresh capital commitments so they’ll have money to invest if the market cools down.

The problem is, many of these LPs are already over-allocated. LPs traditionally invest in many asset classes, such as public equities, and they allocate a small percentage of their portfolio to venture capital. Suddenly, they’re finding they’ve forked over more than they’d intended to VCs.

There are several reasons for this situation. First, VCs are returning to them ever faster for more capital  — sometimes in less than two years’ time  — because they are in vesting at such a furious pace.

In a recent development, compounding the problem, not all LPs have received returns from their VC investments that they can recycle into new venture capital allocations. In some cases, this capital is still tied up in startups that are raising much more money than in the past and staying private longer. “We have some large exposures to blue chip names where IPOs have been rumored to be coming for a long time already, and now it’s maybe 2021, maybe 2022,” states one manager who asked not to be named. In other cases where startups have gone public, falling prices have prompted VCs to hang on to their shares instead of distribute them.

The result is that LPs are having to cut back on the number of managers they can fund, and that could mean bad news for venture capitalists and startups alike. These LPs don’t have much choice. As the LP explains it, “We have a pretty structured allocation process, and we’re really trying to be creative,” she says. One venture manager who reappeared too rapidly for more money was  “easy to walk away from,” says this person. “Others, we’re having to do financial backflips for them to remain strong partners.” Either way, this LP adds, “We can’t add any new relationships right now,” meaning new venture teams in particular are out of luck. “When [VCs] shorten their fundraising cycle by nine months to a year, you can only squeeze the balloon so much.”.

Industry observers note that softBank’s $100 billion “Vision Fund” is one substantial reason LPs find themselves in their current predicament. From the moment SoftBank began waving money around several years ago, it rolled out a vicious cycle. According to Chris Douvos, whose investment firm, Ahoy Capital, owns stakes in such venture funds as True Ventures and First Round Capital, “When Andreessen Horowitz hit the scene a decade ago, they changed the tempo of investing and everyone got more aggressive in their dealmaking as a response. Then SoftBank entered the picture in a big way, and it was like a16z on steroids.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

According to recent reports, microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an key point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he stated most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which notes it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

Sources indicate that his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

It has been revealed that he gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed manufacturer that wants to build in Finland. Google declared a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, mentioned he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a major technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

It has been revealed that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the organization for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate firm, and remarked Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

Industry observers note that white House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

According to recent reports, smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

It has been revealed that he put the ballroom donation in the first category, and mentioned the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for problems it considered crucial.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he mentioned much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

#134405. Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1147 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Using AI as an Excuse for Layoffs. Here’s How to Use AI to Retain Talent Instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • According to recent reports, when a company introduces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first.
  • AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, when a company introduces layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

There is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a company needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

That distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people swiftly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

In a recent development, there is another way to implement AI. Start by asking how it can make your people more capable.

I learned this lesson long before the current AI boom. When we were building Amazon Web Services, talented engineers were spending too much time provisioning servers, configuring storage and handling infrastructure before they could get to the work they were actually there to do. By removing that friction, we gave developers more capacity to build, experiment and solve customer problems.

Industry observers note that I saw the same principle years later with a junior attorney who spent hours researching and formatting before reaching the work that required her judgment. Generative AI could produce a first draft in minutes, giving her more time to refine the facts and shape the narrative for the client’s best outcome.

That is the opportunity leaders should look for with AI. Before calculating how many positions an efficiency gain could eliminate, ask what your people could accomplish if repetitive work stopped consuming so much of their day.

In a recent development, suppose AI gives a team back 10 or 20% of its capacity. What happens to that time?

It could be the customer follow-up that keeps getting postponed, an improvement sitting in the backlog or a relationship that needs more attention. Those opportunities already exist inside most businesses. The problem is that people have been too busy with repetitive work to pursue them.

Industry observers note that I saw this with a team of customer service agents who spent a significant portion of their day filling out forms and navigating cumbersome systems. An AI tool automated part of that process and gave them roughly an hour back each day.

Recent findings suggest that leadership could have used that hour to justify a smaller team. Instead, employees spent more time connecting with customers, strengthening relationships and solving more complex problems. AI removed work they disliked and created room for work where they could contribute more.

According to recent reports, retaining talent requires planning for people at the beginning of an AI initiative rather than after deployment. If leaders automate first and ask what happens to employees later, the priority is already clear.

It has been revealed that before introducing AI, divide the work into three categories. Some tasks contain little meaningful judgment and can be automated. Others can be accelerated by AI while still requiring human judgment. A third group should remain primarily human because relationships, creativity or judgment create the value. Then make the next decision before deploying anything. Where will the recovered capacity go?

Recent findings suggest that that could mean moving people toward customer relationships, product development, higher-level analysis or other work that contributes more directly to growth. The destination will vary by organization, but leaders should know where they want people to go before technology begins changing their roles.

How you introduce AI also shapes whether employees embrace or resist it. If the first message people hear is that a tool will save 40% of their time, they may immediately wonder what leadership plans to do with that 40%.

Recent findings suggest that tell employees which frustrating work you want to reduce. Show them what they will have more time to accomplish. Explain how their roles can become more valuable as AI handles repetitive tasks.

Then demonstrate that commitment through what happens next. If employees see recovered time consistently reinvested into better work, stronger skills and new opportunities, AI starts to look like a tool they can use rather than a threat they need to survive.

According to recent reports, leaders can begin before buying another AI tool. Take one team and map how AI could change its work, then answer these four questions together before deployment.

Industry observers note that 1. What work should disappear? Break roles into individual tasks and identify repetitive work that consumes time without requiring significant human judgment. Focus first on removing friction rather than removing positions.

In a recent development, 2. What human capability should grow? For every task AI can automate or accelerate, identify what employees could do with the recovered time. Look for work involving customers, relationships, creativity, problem-solving or judgment.

3. Where will the recovered capacity go? Give those hours a destination before deployment. If AI saves a team eight hours each week, decide whether those hours will go toward customer service, innovation, newly introduced revenue opportunities or another measurable priority.

Sources indicate that 4. What will you tell employees? Explain what AI will take off their plates and what you want them doing more of as a result. Managers should be able to describe that future clearly before asking employees to adopt the technology.

AI will change jobs, and some roles will change significantly as companies redesign how work gets done. But leaders still control a critical decision about what they do with the capacity AI creates.

Before treating efficiency as a reason to reduce headcount, ask what your people could accomplish with the time they get back. The companies that answer that question first have an opportunity to use AI for something far more valuable than cutting costs. They can use it to build a more capable workforce.

Recent findings suggest that when a tech giant reveals layoffs and points to AI, I always want to know what happened first. Did the technology fundamentally change how work gets done, or did leadership already need to reduce costs and AI became a convenient explanation?

It has been revealed that there is a meaningful difference. AI can automate tasks, accelerate workflows and change the skills a manufacturer needs. But AI does not walk into a boardroom and decide how many people should remain employed. Leaders decide what happens to the capacity the technology creates.

It has been revealed that that distinction matters because employees are watching. If every AI announcement is followed by layoffs, people quickly learn that greater efficiency puts their jobs at risk and they have little reason to embrace the tools leadership wants them to use.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

Industry News: webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • Recent findings suggest that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Recent findings suggest that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight consumers want to hear.

According to recent reports, on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It claims TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Industry observers note that read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

According to recent reports, the AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card highlights the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 fresh tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Recent findings suggest that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

It has been revealed that overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

In a recent development, the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary launched his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his tech giant a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The firm recently shifted again, adding a newly introduced line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary noted, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

In a recent development, high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the complications.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

Recent findings suggest that when I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

Recent findings suggest that my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

Industry observers note that I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [Newly introduced York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

According to recent reports, in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

According to recent reports, nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

In a recent development, my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

#134400. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month.
  • The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging.
  • Recent findings suggest that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk remarked it wouldn’t even have a plug.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

Recent findings suggest that when Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk remarked it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

That blueprint didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger glitch is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

According to recent reports, for a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”.

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

Recent findings suggest that so you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Sources indicate that tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Recent findings suggest that tesla’s own looks for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

In a recent development, the other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

Recent findings suggest that this is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

According to recent reports, musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also mentioned “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

Industry observers note that that saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

In a recent development, I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

In a recent development, will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it introduces, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. Despite the sharp fall in the cryptocurrency market, Michael Saylor-led Strategy has not stopped its Bitcoin (BTC) buying spree, as it picked up 457 BTC worth around $29.6 million.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

The latest data from Strategy's SEC filing reveals that the firm has bought 457 Bitcoin at an average price of $64,898 per coin.

The new purchase brings Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings to around 851,305 BTC, which accounts for over 4% of the cryptocurrency's maximum supply of 21 million coins.

The firm has now spent around $64.23 billion to build its Bitcoin holdings at an average price of $75,446 per Bitcoin.

It is worth noting that Strategy has been buying BTC at gradually decreasing prices as the cryptocurrency market continues to bleed heavily.

On Nov. 2, the firm declared that it had bought 811 BTC, worth around $65.5 million, at an average price of $80,846 per Bitcoin.

A week later, on Nov. 9, Strategy announced the purchase of 1,036 BTC worth $81.9 million at an average price of $79,012.

The firm’s Bitcoin purchase a week later, on Nov. 16, was relatively smaller at 485 BTC, worth $33.4 million, with an average price of $68,887.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced 457 BTC purchase continues this pattern. The latest Strategy purchase was made at an almost 20% lower price than the firm’s Nov. 2 acquisition.

Overall, the firm has made four weekly purchases, scooping up around 2,789 BTC worth $210.4 million.

According to recent reports, however, these purchases have been much smaller than before. The latest $29.6 million purchase is almost 64% lower than the $81.9 million purchase revealed just two weeks ago.

Although Saylor is doubling down on Bitcoin, Strategy’s massive holdings in the cryptocurrency are underwater as the market has been struggling to regain its footing.

In a recent development, on Nov. 21, Bitcoin hit a low of around $55,130, its lowest level since September 2024, before rebounding above $61,000.

The firm’s recent purchases have helped reduce its overall average Bitcoin acquisition cost, but the drop has not been that significant.

For example, with the latest purchase, the average cost of the firm’s Bitcoin holdings dropped from $75,452 to around $75,446, a decline of just $6 per Bitcoin.

At the same time, the firm has also been putting a lot of resources into supporting its preferred securities.

In the latest reporting period, Strategy sold around 1.93 million common shares, raising net proceeds of $176.7 million.

The CEO is hardly alone in intentionally or otherwise sowing confusion around his credentials, however. Over the years, we’ve mistakenly believed that a number of founders have obtained specific college degrees based on their LinkedIn bio, only to learn offline that they enrolled for some period of time in a particular program that they didn’t complete.

It happened most recently with the cofounder of a startup who one would might surmise based on his LinkedIn profile has a master’s degree from Harvard but does not. We also misunderstood the CEO of a robotics company to have a PhD based on her LinkedIn. It was our fault; it mentioned under the credit that she’d left to start a company. But anyone scanning the site might have come to the same wrong conclusion. (We pointed this out to her team, and mention of the PhD was deleted.).

In a higher-profile case, James Damore, the fired Google engineer who authored that infamous memo about the company’s diversity practices and whose LinkedIn page cited under “Education” a “PhD, Systems Biology,” removed mention of those doctoral studies after Wired confirmed with Harvard that he was enrolled in the program but didn’t complete the doctorate.

Damore tried to defend his own LinkedIn profile, tweeting at the time, “I never told anyone I have a PhD. LinkedIn can’t distinguish between being in the PhD program and having a PhD (I forgot to update it).”.

Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Sources indicate that amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

It has been revealed that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the organization’s earnings call last month.

Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

It has been revealed that decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” mentioned Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Recent findings suggest that decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

According to recent reports, amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon stated last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other massive buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

The firm stated that the board was satisfied with Huang's "candor and ability to lead" after a series of meetings with him, and that its independent investigation would continue. According to the company, the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and on Nov. 17, during the company's earnings call, Jones remarked that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

According to recent reports, in premarket trading, Nvidia stock jumped 27% to $159.48 as of 9 a.m. ET, and at the start of U.S. trading on Monday, Nvidia shares were up more than 30%. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 2:39 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 6:55 am.

— Muralidhar Krishnaprasad has been named as vice president of analytics, storage and databases at Amazon Web Services, a role that reports to AWS CEO Matt Garman. Krishnaprasad, who goes by MK, left Salesforce after eight years. He was president and chief technology officer there, where he helped build the organization’s agentic enterprise platform.

At AWS, he will lead an organization that unites Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), database and analytics services.

“MK brings deep technical roots, a customer-obsessed mindset and experience building data platforms at global scale,” Garman said in an email to staff.

Earlier in his career, MK spent more than a decade each at Oracle and Microsoft.

US Strikes Back After $6 Billion Binance Hack

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (455 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.
  • 23 announcement, the DOJ said that it has filed a civil forfeiture complaint to recover over $1.1 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as part of its efforts to retrieve the billions lost in the massive hack.
  • In a recent development, the recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.

As per a Nov. 23 announcement, the DOJ said that it has filed a civil forfeiture complaint to recover over $1.1 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as part of its efforts to retrieve the billions lost in the massive hack.

In a recent development, the recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct. 29 in one of the biggest crypto heists ever.

Recent findings suggest that the DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

The assets are alleged to have been stolen from Binance and laundered by North Korean cybercriminals.

Industry observers note that significantly, the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government earlier this month. With the fresh court filing, the potential recovery of the assets has taken another step forward.

The DOJ further claimed that U.S. authorities have successfully helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency since the attack in October.

This is nearly half of the total $6 billion-plus stolen from Binance, though the government did not provide details about how much of that has been returned to the exchange.

According to recent reports, the importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and crypto firms to ensure that hackers don't get away with stolen assets was stressed by Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

Industry observers note that “North Korean cyber hackers stole over $6 billion of cryptocurrency from Binance. But prompt coordination with both the government and our private sector partners helped to avoid the bulk of these assets from being lost,” Duva mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that U.S. authorities have further revealed the sophisticated money laundering techniques used by North Korean hackers to conceal their stolen cryptocurrency.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said that the regime uses intricate money laundering methods to convert stolen digital assets into funds for its illicit activities.

After the Binance hack, authorities quickly worked to trace the stolen funds and coordinate with crypto service providers to block further transfers.

The U.S. Secret Service claimed that its investigators were able to detect and freeze some of the stolen funds within minutes of the hack.

Industry observers note that "The bad actors in this intrusion thought they could run from law enforcement. They've found out they were wrong," stated Secret Service Special Agent in Charge Todd Bratz.

What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • It has been revealed that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data reveals.
  • According to recent reports, to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

It has been revealed that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data reveals. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

According to recent reports, to get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Industry observers note that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

In a recent development, by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old manufacturer raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

According to recent reports, san Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor notes it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

According to recent reports, the next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Sources indicate that of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old organization picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

According to recent reports, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual company highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.
